deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E260 Euler models fluid friction as a resistance proportional to the local pressure, including the weight of the atmosphere l (about 30 ft of water), with friction coefficient alpha. Integrating the steady one-dimensional momentum balance along each straight tube piece then gives exponential factors of the form B = e^{-alpha b/g}, where b is the piece length and g relates to its cross-section gg.

§94 compares two ways of bringing water to the same point C. In the earlier example (§§86-87) water ran from a vessel 100 ft high through a horizontal tube 100 ft long. Here the vessel height a is negligible and the water runs down a tube inclined at 45 degrees. The data are gg = 1/100 sq ft (g = 1/10 ft), cos zeta = 1/sqrt2 and length b = 100 sqrt2 ft.

§95: alpha b/g = 0.3536 (this implies alpha = 1/4000), so B = e^{-0.3536} = 0.7021, which is correct (0.7022). The outlet kk is taken very small and a is negligible. The formula from §93, in the form v = aB + (1-B)(g cos zeta/alpha - l), then gives the efflux head. Numerically this is 0.2979 x (400/sqrt2 - 30) = 0.2979 x 252.8, about 75.3 ft. Here g cos zeta/alpha = 4000 x 0.1/sqrt2 and l = 30 ft is the atmospheric head.

Without friction the head would be 100 ft. In the previous case (horizontal tube, 100-ft reservoir) it was only 5 2/3 ft. Euler concludes the water will rise higher with the inclined arrangement. Under his law this follows because pressure, and hence friction, stays low all along the descending tube, while in the horizontal tube it is high throughout.

Case V (§96) sets up a new problem. A vessel AB has negligible height a and very large area ff. The delivery tube has section gg. A vertical riser CD has height c and section hh, and the outlet DD has area kk. Two variants are treated:
- (i) a straight tube BE of length b inclined at zeta to the vertical;
- (ii) a bent tube bcE whose two straight legs have lengths b cos zeta and b sin zeta.
Euler puts G = k^4/g^4 and H = k^4/h^4. The solutions follow on the next page (§§97-98) by composing the exponential transfer factors of the successive straight pieces.
errors: Printed b = 100 sqrt2 '= 14,14 ped.' should be 141,4 ft (the decimal point is misplaced).

The bracket printed (as transcribed) as (100/sqrt2 - 30) must be (400/sqrt2 - 30), i.e. g cos zeta/alpha = 4000 x 0.1/sqrt2. With 100/sqrt2 the product would be about 12.1, not 75.3. Either a misprint or a misreading of the superscript.
75.309 is slightly off: 0.2979 x 252.84 = 75.32. This is a minor arithmetic slip.
In §96, 'amplitudo CC = bb' and 'k^4/b^4' should read hh and h^4, since the next page uses h and the gothic h. Possibly a print/OCR confusion of b and h.
The catchword '67. His' should be '97. His'.

Physically, the whole computation rests on Euler's assumption that friction is proportional to pressure, including atmospheric pressure. This is wrong for fluids, where resistance depends on velocity. Conclusions such as the effect of atmospheric weight on flow are artefacts of that law.

ideas.what: Pipe friction proportional to local pressure (including atmospheric head), producing exponential attenuation factors e^{-alpha b/g} along each straight tube segment
ideas.modern_name: Pressure-dependent (Coulomb-type) wall friction in 1-D pipe flow; superseded by velocity-dependent head-loss laws (Chezy, Darcy-Weisbach)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler's own (abandoned) hypothesis in E260; correct laws: Chezy (1770s), Darcy-Weisbach (19th c.)
ideas.where_published: E260 itself; discussed in Truesdell's introductions to Opera Omnia ser. II vols 12-13 (unsure of exact page)

ideas.what: Numerical comparison: delivery by an inclined descending tube gives a higher efflux head than a horizontal tube fed by a tall reservoir
ideas.modern_name: Worked example of head loss in pipe networks

ideas.what: Composition of straight tube segments (inclined vs bent), each contributing an exponential factor, for a system ending in a vertical riser
ideas.modern_name: Series composition of transfer factors / head losses in pipe networks

deep.surprise_reason: A routine numerical illustration within Euler's known, and since abandoned, pressure-proportional friction theory, plus the setup of another case. Only misprints are of note.
transcription_corrections: '=14,14 ped.' is as printed but mathematically should be 141,4.
'(100/sqrt2 - 30)': the superscript should likely be read as 400. In any case 400 is required for the stated result 75.309.
'amplitudo CC=bb' should probably be hh (and gothic H = k^4/h^4 rather than k^4/b^4), consistent with the next page.
Catchword '67. His' is a misprint for '97. His'.
